figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Single- and multi-input multi-turn editing. TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over editing turns while retaining the base model’s (FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B) editing capability.
figures.headline: Repeated edits drift in the base model, while TailSteer keeps cumulative drift low across turns and retains editing ability.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 1, repeated editing can wash out fine textures, alter non-target object or facial details, distort background structures, and eventually produce visible artifacts.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Trajectory tail remains correctable. Low-frequency content is recovered early, whereas higher-frequency details are primarily recovered near the tail (top), while preservation error in unchanged regions continues to decrease but remains non-zero at the endpoint (bottom).
figures.headline: Preservation error keeps falling toward the endpoint but stays nonzero, while high-frequency similarity rises sharply near the tail.
citing_sentences: Fig. 2 reveals that low-frequency similarity is already high before the final steps, whereas higher-frequency similarity rises sharply near the tail.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Data curation of preservation-aware trajectory endpoints. We construct supervision from rollouts of the frozen base editor using two complementary edit types: (a) identity editing provides full-image preservation trajectories, while (b) local editing provides partial-preservation trajectories with spatially localized changes. Only samples that pass the corresponding sanity checks are retained and cached as training trajectories for subsequent TailSteer optimization.
figures.headline: Identity and local editing rollouts from the frozen base editor yield preservation masks and endpoints after sanity filtering.
citing_sentences: To obtain reliable supervision, we construct two complementary trajectory types in which the resulting edit is expected to preserve part of the source image, identity editing and local editing, as illustrated in Fig. 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: One-step terminal intervention: benefits and limitations. (a) We fine-tune FLUX.2-klein-9B with supervision only at the final sampling step, steering from the cached pre-terminal state $x_{\tau}^{\mathrm{base}}$ toward the preservation-aware target $x_{1}^{\mathrm{tgt}}$. (b) The base model accumulates visible identity drift over repeated edits (top row). Applying the fine-tuned model only at the final step markedly improves long-horizon preservation (middle row), whereas using it throughout sampling causes desaturation and detail loss (bottom row). Therefore, it is necessary to preserve the earlier dynamics.
figures.headline: Fine-tuning only the last step reduces identity drift, but applying it at every step desaturates outputs and loses detail.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: On-policy training of TailSteer. At randomly sampled training states $x_{k_{1}}$ and $x_{k_{2}}$, the refined model receives region-dependent supervision. In the prior region, its prediction is matched to the frozen base model’s velocity $v^{\mathrm{base}}$; in the transition region, the target $v^{*}$ progressively blends $v^{\mathrm{base}}$ with the preservation velocity $v^{\mathrm{pres}}$ toward $x_{1}^{\mathrm{tgt}}$. To obtain these states on-policy, the refined model rolls out from the nearest preceding cached anchor in prior region, and from the fixed steering-onset state in transition region. The velocity target is then recomputed at the state actually reached by the refined model, with gradients applied only to its prediction at the sampled step.
figures.headline: Training states come from the refined model's own rollouts, with targets set by base velocity early and blended toward preservation late.
citing_sentences: Importantly, all supervision is constructed on states reached by the refined model’s own denoising rollouts, as illustrated in Fig. 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: 20-turn qualitative comparison. While competing methods exhibit cumulative visual drift, TailSteer faithfully preserves the original tabletop color and previously established details, including the coffee cup, latte art, and cookie on the right, even after 20 successive editing turns.
figures.headline: After 20 turns, TailSteer keeps the tabletop color and earlier details that competing methods lose through cumulative drift.
citing_sentences: Fig. 6 compares TailSteer with training-free MTC (Zhou et al., 2025), video-data-trained VINCIE (Qu et al., 2026), and inference-time preservation modules, including FreqEdit (Liao et al., 2026), VAE-LFA (Wang et al., 2026), and Consistency LoRA V2 (dx8152, 2026).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Multi-input multi-turn editing. TailSteer retains base models’ multi-image editing capabilities while substantially reducing cumulative drift, preserving backgrounds during multi-person and multi-object compositing and the girl’s dress details across successive skeleton-guided edits.
figures.headline: TailSteer keeps backgrounds and the girl's dress details across multi-person, multi-object, and skeleton-guided edits.
citing_sentences: This advantage extends to multi-input editing (as shown in Fig. 7), where TailSteer retains the base models’ compositing and skeleton-guided editing capabilities while better preserving backgrounds and the girl’s dress details across pose changes.

figures.caption: Ablation of training strategies. With the same training data, full TailSteer better balances preserving the base model’s editing capabilities with enhancing multi-turn drift resistance.
figures.headline: Full TailSteer balances editing capability and drift resistance better than standard supervised fine-tuning on the same data.

abstract: Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift. This long-term drift is often mitigated through training on multi-turn data or cross-turn rollouts, potentially altering pretrained priors, or through specialized inference-time mechanisms that are difficult to scale to foundation models. We introduce TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that improves multi-turn robustness while retaining the generative and editing capabilities acquired through earlier training. TailSteer follows a simple principle: keep early denoising dynamics close to those of the base model and concentrate preservation corrections near the trajectory tail, where fine-grained deviations can be suppressed. These corrections are learned from the editor’s own on-policy denoising rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference without requiring curated ground-truth editing pairs. Experiments across the FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen families show that TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15–20 editing turns while largely preserving base-model performance on extensive text-to-image and single-image editing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that long-horizon editing robustness can be unlocked in foundation models after TailSteer, rather than by relearning their existing capabilities. Project page: https://lyricccco.github.io/tailsteer/

sections.body: The introduction argues that each edited output becomes the next input, so small unintended changes are inherited and build up. In the paper's examples, repeated editing washes out fine textures, alters non-target object and facial details, distorts backgrounds, and produces visible artifacts. The authors group existing fixes into three families: auxiliary modules or constraints, changes to the representation space, and explicit cross-turn memory. They say these leave the base model's own behavior under repeated editing largely unchanged. Fig. 2 motivates focusing on the trajectory tail: low-frequency similarity is already high before the final steps, higher-frequency similarity rises sharply near the tail, and preservation error stays nonzero at the endpoint. The section reports no benchmark numbers.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: One-shot editors accumulate small errors across repeated turns, so strong single-turn editing does not guarantee long-horizon editing.

sections.body: Related work groups prior methods into four areas: representation fidelity, inference-time guidance using masks and frequency corrections, feature reuse with visual memory, and multi-turn-specific training. The authors argue that representation designs address representation-level limits rather than denoising dynamics. They also argue that training-free inference procedures may not generalize readily across foundation models. Multi-turn-specific training relies on video-derived sequences or cross-turn reinforcement learning. TailSteer is positioned as improving preservation by refining the existing model's denoising dynamics, without relearning editing behavior from cross-turn supervision. The section cites prior work and reports no experimental results.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior fixes add modules, change representations, or add memory, whereas TailSteer trains the base model's own denoising dynamics.

sections.body:
TailSteer copies the frozen base model into a trainable model and trains it on states reached by its own denoising rollouts. Before a steering onset $k_{s}$, the copy is trained to match the base model's velocity. After it, the target blends the base velocity with a velocity toward a preservation endpoint, and the blend weight falls from 1 at $k_{s}$ to 0 at $\tau$. The endpoint is built from a binary mask that marks unchanged regions, using the source image for those regions:

$$
x_{1}^{\mathrm{tgt}}=M\odot x^{\mathrm{src}}+(1-M)\odot x_{1}^{\mathrm{base}}
$$

Training data come from identity edits and filtered local edits, with no curated ground-truth pairs. At inference the refined model runs the full trajectory alone, with no switching, adapters or extra components.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: TailSteer trains a copy of the base model on its own rollouts, steering only late denoising steps toward source-preserving endpoints.

sections.body: Experiments cover FLUX.1 Kontext [dev], FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT and Qwen-Image-2.1. Each model is trained for 2,000 updates on 11,947 candidate source images. The selected onsets are $k_{s}$ = 25, 46, 42 and 30 for Kontext, Klein, SenseNova and Qwen. Qualitatively, after 20 turns TailSteer keeps the tabletop color and earlier details, while inference-time preservation modules noticeably alter base behavior and degrade single-turn editing, as Table 2 shows. Table 1 reports text-to-image and single-turn scores against each base model. Fig. 8 shows outside-box drift over 10 turns. The section does not report failure cases beyond the stated comparisons.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Across four backbones, TailSteer reduces drift over 15–20 editing turns while keeping single-turn scores close to base models.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that TailSteer is a final-stage training framework. It concentrates preservation corrections near the denoising trajectory tail and retains earlier dynamics. It states that cumulative drift is substantially reduced across successive edits, and that generative capabilities are largely retained across FLUX, SenseNova and Qwen. The authors conclude that multi-turn editing reliability need not be learned anew, and can instead be unlocked by refining how foundation models complete each edit. The conclusion introduces no new experiments and no new numbers.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion says TailSteer reduces cumulative drift across FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen while largely retaining base generative capabilities.
